blocks.p: I told you before how the noble Prince Emmanuel received the prisoners, how they behaved before him, and how he sent them home with pipe and drum going before them. Now you must imagine that those in the town who had all this while been waiting to hear of their deaths could not help being troubled with sadness of mind, and with thoughts that pricked like thorns. Nor could they keep their thoughts fixed on any one point; the wind blew them this way and that in great uncertainty, and their hearts were like a pair of scales jostled by a shaking hand. But at last, looking long over the wall of Mansoul, they thought they saw some people returning to the town, and wondered, Who can they be? Who can they be? At last they made out that it was the prisoners. But can you imagine their wonder, especially when they saw in what style and with what honor they had been sent home? They went down to the camp in black, but they came back to the town in white; they went down to the camp in ropes, they came back in chains of gold; they went down to the camp with their feet in shackles, but came back with their steps set free and wide beneath them; they went to the camp expecting death, but they came back with the assurance of life; they went down to the camp with heavy hearts, but came back with pipe and drum playing before them. So as soon as they reached Eye-gate, the poor, tottering town of Mansoul ventured a shout; and it was such a shout that it made the captains in the Prince’s army jump at the sound. Poor hearts, who could blame them? Their dead friends had come back to life; for it was like life from the dead to see the elders of Mansoul shining in such splendor. They had looked for nothing but the axe and the block; but look: joy and gladness, comfort and consolation, and such sweet music going with them as was enough to make a sick man well.

So when they came up, they greeted one another: “Welcome, welcome! And blessed be the one who spared you!” Then they added, “We see it is well with you. But how will it go with the town of Mansoul? Will it go well with the town of Mansoul?”
Then the Recorder and the Lord Mayor answered them, “Oh, tidings! Glad tidings! Good tidings of good, and of great joy, for poor Mansoul!”

Then the townspeople gave another shout that made the earth ring again. After this they asked more particularly how things had gone in the camp, and what message the men brought from Emmanuel. So they told them all that had happened at the camp, and everything the Prince had done for them; and this made Mansoul marvel at the wisdom and grace of Prince Emmanuel. Then they told what they had received at his hands for the whole town, and the Recorder delivered it in these words: “PARDON, PARDON, PARDON for Mansoul! And Mansoul shall know it tomorrow!” Then he gave the order, and they went and summoned Mansoul to meet in the market-place the next day, to hear their general pardon read.

But who can imagine what a turn, what a change, what a transformation even this hint of things made in the face of the town of Mansoul! No one in Mansoul could sleep that night for joy. In every house there was joy and music, singing and making merry; telling and hearing of Mansoul’s happiness was all that Mansoul had to do; and this was the refrain of all their songs: “Oh, more of this at sunrise! More of this tomorrow!”

“Who would have thought yesterday,” one would say, “that today would be such a day for us? And who would have thought, seeing our prisoners go down in irons, that they would come back in chains of gold? Yes, the very men who judged themselves as they went to be judged by their judge were acquitted by his own mouth, not because they were innocent, but by the Prince’s mercy, and sent home with pipe and drum. But is this the usual custom of princes? Do they make a habit of showing such favors to traitors? No! This belongs to Shaddai alone, and to Emmanuel his Son!”

Now the morning came on quickly; so the Lord Mayor, the Lord Willbewill, and the Recorder came down at the appointed time to the market-place, where the townspeople were waiting. They came in the clothing and the glory the Prince had put on them the day before, and the street was lit up with their glory. So the Mayor, the Recorder, and my Lord Willbewill went down to Mouth-gate, at the lower end of the market-place, because from old times that was where public matters were read aloud. There they came in their robes, with drums going before them; and the people were very eager to hear the whole of the matter.

Then the Recorder stood up, and first beckoning with his hand for silence, he read out the pardon in a loud voice. But when he came to these words, “The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin; and to them every kind of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven” [Exod. 34:6-7; Matt. 12:31], and so on, they could not keep from leaping for joy. For you must understand that the name of every man in Mansoul was written into it; and the seals of the pardon made a splendid show.

When the Recorder had finished reading the pardon, the townsmen ran up onto the walls of the town and leaped and skipped there for joy, and bowed themselves seven times with their faces toward Emmanuel’s pavilion, and shouted aloud for joy, “Long live Emmanuel forever!” Then the young men of Mansoul were ordered to ring the bells for joy. So the bells rang, and the people sang, and the music played in every house in Mansoul.

Now when the Prince had sent the three prisoners home with joy, and with pipe and drum, he had commanded his captains, with all the field officers and soldiers of his army, to be ready on the morning of the reading of the pardon, to carry out his further pleasure. So that morning, just as the Recorder finished reading the pardon, Emmanuel commanded that all the trumpets in the camp should sound, and that the colors should be displayed, half of them on Mount Gracious and half on Mount Justice. He commanded also that all the captains should show themselves in full armor, and that the soldiers should shout for joy. Nor was Captain Credence silent on such a day, though he was in the castle; from the top of the stronghold he showed himself, with a blast of the trumpet, to Mansoul and to the Prince’s camp.
Thus I have shown you the manner and the way that Emmanuel took to recover the town of Mansoul from under the hand and power of the tyrant Diabolus.

When the Prince had finished these outward ceremonies of his joy, he commanded his captains and soldiers to show Mansoul some feats of war, and they set about it at once. But oh, with what agility, nimbleness, skill, and daring these military men displayed their arts of war to the town of Mansoul, which now stood gazing at them!

They marched, they countermarched; they opened to the right and left; they divided and subdivided; they closed, they wheeled, they secured their front and rear with their right and left wings, and twenty things more, all with such precision, and then were all back in their places as before, that they took, no, they carried away, the hearts of everyone in Mansoul who watched. And add to this the handling of their arms and the management of their weapons of war, which were marvelously captivating to Mansoul, and to me.

When this display was over, the whole town of Mansoul came out as one man to the Prince in the camp, to thank and praise him for his abundant favor, and to beg him to come into Mansoul with his men and make his quarters there forever. They did this most humbly, bowing seven times to the ground before him.
Then he said, “All peace be to you.”

So the town came near and touched the top of his golden scepter with their hands, and they said, “Oh, that Prince Emmanuel, with his captains and men of war, would live in Mansoul forever, and that his battering rams and slings might be lodged in her, for the use and service of the Prince and for the help and strength of Mansoul! For we have room for you, we have room for your men, we have room for your weapons of war too, and a place to make a storehouse for your baggage. Do it, Emmanuel, and you shall be King and Captain in Mansoul forever. Yes, govern too according to all the desire of your heart, and make your captains and men of war governors and princes under you, and we will become your servants, and your laws shall be our direction.”

They added a further plea for His Majesty to consider. “For,” they said, “if now, after all this grace given to us, your miserable town of Mansoul, you should withdraw from us, you and your captains, the town of Mansoul will die. Yes, our blessed Emmanuel, if you should leave us now, after you have done us so much good and shown us so much mercy, what will follow but that our joy will be as though it had never been, and our enemies will come on us a second time with more rage than the first? So we beg you, O desire of our eyes, the strength and life of our poor town, accept this proposal we now make to our Lord: come and live among us, and let us be your people. Besides, Lord, for all we know many Diabolonians may still be lurking in the town of Mansoul to this day, and when you leave us they will betray us into the hand of Diabolus again; and who knows what schemes, plots, or contrivances have already passed between them about this? We dread falling into his horrible hands again. So please accept our palace as your residence, and the houses of the best men in our town for lodging your soldiers and their equipment.”
Then the Prince said, “If I come into your town, will you allow me to carry further what is in my heart against my enemies and yours? Yes, will you help me in such undertakings?”

They answered, “We do not know what we will do. We never once thought we would have been such traitors to Shaddai as we have proved to be. What, then, shall we say to our Lord? Let him put no trust in his saints [Job 15:15]; let the Prince live in our castle and make our town a garrison; let him set his noble captains and his warlike soldiers over us; yes, let him conquer us with his love and overcome us with his grace, and then surely he will be with us and help us, as he was with us and as he helped us on the morning our pardon was read to us. We will go along with our Lord and with his ways, and stand with his word against the mighty.

“One word more, and your servants are done and will trouble our Lord no further. We do not know the depth of your wisdom, our Prince. Who, ruled by his own reason, could ever have thought that so much sweetness as we now enjoy could have come out of the bitter trials we were tried with at first? But, Lord, let light go before and love come after; yes, take us by the hand and lead us by your counsels, and let this always rest on us, that all things will turn out for the best for your servants. Come to our Mansoul and do as you please. Or, Lord, come to our Mansoul and do whatever you will, so long as you keep us from sinning and make us useful to Your Majesty.”

Then the Prince said to the town of Mansoul again, “Go, return to your houses in peace. I will gladly grant your desire in this. I will move my royal pavilion; I will draw up my forces before Eye-gate tomorrow, and so march on into the town of Mansoul. I will take possession of your castle of Mansoul and set my soldiers over you. Yes, I will yet do things in Mansoul that cannot be matched in any nation, country, or kingdom under heaven.”

Then the men of Mansoul gave a shout and went home in peace, and told their families and friends the good that Emmanuel had promised. “And tomorrow,” they said, “he will march into our town and take up his dwelling in Mansoul, he and his men.”

Then the people of Mansoul hurried out to the green trees and the meadows to gather branches and flowers, to strew the streets for their Prince, the Son of Shaddai, when he came. They made garlands and other fine decorations to show how joyful they were, and would be, to receive their Emmanuel. They strewed the street all the way from Eye-gate to the castle gate, the place where the Prince was to stay. And they got ready whatever music the town could provide, to play before him all the way to the palace, his home.

So at the appointed time he made his approach to Mansoul, and the gates were set open for him; and there the elders and leaders of Mansoul met him to greet him with a thousand welcomes. Then he rose and entered Mansoul, he and all his servants. The elders of Mansoul went dancing before him until he came to the castle gates. And this was the manner of his going up: he was dressed in his golden armor, he rode in his royal chariot, the trumpets sounded around him, the colors were displayed, his ten thousands went up at his feet, and the elders of Mansoul danced before him. And now the walls of the famous town of Mansoul were filled with the trampling feet of its people, who had gone up to watch the blessed Prince and his royal army approach. The windows, balconies, and rooftops too were all filled with people of every sort, come to see their town being filled with good.

When he had come as far into the town as the Recorder’s house, he sent to Captain Credence to learn whether the castle of Mansoul was ready to receive his royal presence (for its preparation had been left to that captain), and word came back that it was. Then Captain Credence was commanded to come out with his forces to meet the Prince; this was done as he had commanded, and the captain escorted him into the castle. This done, the Prince lodged that night in the castle with his mighty captains and men of war, to the joy of the town of Mansoul.

The townspeople’s next concern was how the Prince’s captains and soldiers should be quartered among them; and the question was not how to keep them out, but how to fill their houses with them; for every man in Mansoul now held Emmanuel and his men in such esteem that nothing grieved them more than that their houses were not big enough for each of them to take in the Prince’s whole army. They counted it their glory to wait on them, and in those days they would run at their bidding like errand boys.
At last they settled it this way:
1. Captain Innocency was to be quartered at Mr. Reason’s.
2. Captain Patience was to be quartered at Mr. Mind’s. (This Mr. Mind had been the Lord Willbewill’s clerk in the time of the late rebellion.)
3. Captain Charity was ordered to be quartered at Mr. Affection’s house.

4. Captain Good-hope was to be quartered at my Lord Mayor’s. As for the Recorder’s house, the Recorder himself asked (because his house was next to the castle, and because the Prince had ordered that, if need arose, the alarm should be given to Mansoul from him), I say, he himself asked that Captain Boanerges and Captain Conviction should take up their quarters with him, they and all their men.

5. As for Captain Judgment and Captain Execution, my Lord Willbewill took them and their men in, because he was now to rule under the Prince for the good of the town of Mansoul, as he had ruled before under the tyrant Diabolus for its harm and damage.
6. Emmanuel’s other forces were quartered throughout the rest of the town; but Captain Credence and his men stayed on in the castle.
So the Prince, his captains, and his soldiers were lodged in the town of Mansoul.

Now the elders and leaders of Mansoul felt they could never have enough of Prince Emmanuel; his person, his actions, his words, and his bearing were so pleasing, so winning, so desirable to them. So they begged him that, though the castle of Mansoul was his residence (and they wished he might live there forever), he would often visit the streets, houses, and people of Mansoul. “For,” they said, “dread Sovereign, your presence, your looks, your smiles, your words, are the life and strength and sinews of the town of Mansoul.”

Besides this, they asked that they might have continual access to him, without difficulty or interruption (and for that very purpose he commanded that the gates should stand open), so that they might see there the manner of his doings, the fortifications of the place, and the royal mansion of the Prince.
When he spoke, they all closed their mouths and listened; and when he walked, it was their delight to copy him in his goings.

Now on one occasion Emmanuel made a feast for the town of Mansoul, and on the feast day the townspeople came to the castle to share his banquet. He feasted them with every kind of food from far away: food that never grew in the fields of Mansoul, nor in the whole Kingdom of Universe; it was food that came from his Father’s court. Dish after dish was set before them, and they were told to eat freely; but whenever a fresh dish came, they would whisper to one another, “What is it?” for they did not know what to call it. They drank also of the water that was made wine, and were very merry with him. There was music the whole time at the table; and man ate the food of angels, and was given honey out of the rock. [Ps. 78:25; 81:16] So Mansoul ate the food that belonged to the court alone; yes, now they had their fill of it.

I must not forget to tell you that, though there were musicians at this table, they were not musicians of the country, nor of the town of Mansoul; they were the masters of the songs that were sung at the court of Shaddai.

After the feast, Emmanuel wanted to entertain the town of Mansoul with some curious riddles of secrets, drawn up by his Father’s Secretary through the skill and wisdom of Shaddai; there are none like them in any kingdom. These riddles were made about King Shaddai himself, and about Emmanuel his Son, and about his wars and dealings with Mansoul.

Emmanuel also explained some of those riddles to them himself; and oh, how their minds were lit up! They saw what they had never seen; they could never have thought that such rare things could be hidden in so few and such ordinary words. I told you whom these riddles concerned, and as they were opened the people plainly saw it. Yes, they gathered that the things themselves were a kind of portrait, and a portrait of Emmanuel himself; for when they read in the chart where the riddles were written, and then looked into the face of the Prince, the one looked so like the other that Mansoul could not help crying out, “This is the lamb! This is the sacrifice! This is the rock! This is the red heifer! This is the door! And this is the way!” with a great many other things besides.

And so he dismissed the town of Mansoul. Can you imagine how the townspeople were taken with it? Oh, they were carried away with joy, they were drowned in wonder, as they saw and understood and considered what their Emmanuel had entertained them with, and what mysteries he had opened to them. At home in their houses, in their most private places, they could not help singing of him and of his deeds. Yes, the townsmen were now so taken with their Prince that they would sing of him in their sleep.

Now it was in the heart of Prince Emmanuel to remodel the town of Mansoul, and to put it into the condition that would please him most and best serve the profit and security of the now flourishing town of Mansoul. He provided too against uprisings at home and invasions from abroad, such was the love he had for the famous town of Mansoul.

First of all he commanded that the great slings that had been brought from his Father’s court, when he came to the war for Mansoul, should be mounted, some on the battlements of the castle and some on the towers; for there were towers in the town of Mansoul now, towers newly built by Emmanuel since he came. There was also an engine, invented by Emmanuel, made to throw stones from the castle of Mansoul out through Mouth-gate: an engine that could not be resisted, and that never missed its mark. Because of the wonderful exploits it did when it was used, it went without a name; and it was entrusted to the care and management of the brave captain, Captain Credence, in case of war.

Then Emmanuel called the Lord Willbewill and gave him charge of the gates, the wall, and the towers in Mansoul. The Prince also put the militia into his hand, with a special charge to put down all uprisings and riots that might be raised in Mansoul against the peace of our Lord the King, and against the peace and quiet of the town of Mansoul. He also commissioned him, if he found any Diabolonians lurking in any corner of the famous town of Mansoul, to arrest them at once and hold them, or commit them to safe custody, so that they could be proceeded against according to law.

Then he called to him the Lord Understanding, who was the old Lord Mayor, the one put out of office when Diabolus took the town; and he restored him to his former office, and it became his post for life. He told him also to build himself a palace near Eye-gate, and to build it in the form of a tower for defense. And he told him to read in the Revelation of Mysteries all the days of his life, so that he would know how to perform his office rightly.

He also made Mr. Knowledge the Recorder: not out of any contempt for old Mr. Conscience, who had been Recorder before, but because it was in his princely mind to give Mr. Conscience another employment, of which, he told the old gentleman, he would learn more later.

Then he commanded that the image of Diabolus be taken down from where it had been set up and destroyed utterly, beaten into powder and scattered to the wind outside the town wall; and that the image of Shaddai his Father should be set up again, together with his own, on the castle gates; and that it should be more finely drawn than ever, since both his Father and he himself had come to Mansoul in more grace and mercy than before. He wished also that his name should be finely engraved on the front of the town, and done in the best gold, for the honor of the town of Mansoul.

After this was done, Emmanuel gave orders that those three great Diabolonians should be arrested: the two late Lord Mayors, namely Mr. Incredulity and Mr. Lustings, and Mr. Forget-good, the Recorder. Besides these, there were some whom Diabolus had made burgesses and aldermen, members of the town’s council, in Mansoul; and these were committed to prison by the hand of the now valiant and now truly noble, the brave Lord Willbewill.

And these were their names: Alderman Atheism, Alderman Hard-heart, and Alderman False-peace. The burgesses were Mr. No-truth, Mr. Pitiless, Mr. Haughty, and others like them. These were committed to close custody, and the jailer’s name was Mr. True-man. This True-man was one of those Emmanuel had brought with him from his Father’s court when he first made war on Diabolus in the town of Mansoul.

After this, the Prince gave orders that the three strongholds the Diabolonians had built in Mansoul at the command of Diabolus should be demolished and pulled down completely; you read of these strongholds and their names, with their captains and governors, a little before. This took a long time, because of the size of the places, and because the stones, the timber, the iron, and all the rubble had to be carried out of the town.

When this was done, the Prince gave orders that the Lord Mayor and aldermen of Mansoul should call a court of justice for the trial and execution of the Diabolonians in the town, who were now in the keeping of Mr. True-man, the jailer.
